workflow.h2: Six stages between an idea and a garment.
workflow.sub: Most classes stop at stage three. The two that decide whether a design ships are 04 and 05 — reading a failed sample, and correcting the file instead of compensating at the machine.
workflow.s1d: Read artwork the way the trade reads it: technique, scale, material, and what the fabric will allow.
workflow.s2d: Build the file in emCAD — stitch types, underlay, density and the travel order the head will follow.
workflow.s3d: Frame, thread, tension and needle chosen for this cloth. Setup is where half of all faults are decided.
workflow.s4d: Run a sample and read it honestly: puckering, gaps, registration, thread breaks.
workflow.s5d: Fix the file, not the symptom. An operator who slows the head down ships the fault anyway.
workflow.s6d: Run the job, finish the piece, and know why it came out right.
workflow.note: Every course teaches all six stages for its technique. That is the difference between learning a machine and learning the work.

problems.h2: The problems we teach you to solve.
problems.sub: If you already run a machine, you have met most of these. Each one has a cause, and the cause is teachable.
problems.p1c: Needle, thread and material are not matched — and the tension is set for a different cloth. Learn the combinations before you learn the machine.
problems.p2f: It looks right on screen and fails on fabric.
problems.p2c: Density, underlay and path direction. A design is not finished when it looks good; it is finished when it survives the cloth.
problems.p3f: Sequence and beadwork land out of register.
problems.p3c: Framing, travel order and correction. The hoop moves — the file has to be built expecting it.
problems.p4f: The operator compensates for a bad file.
problems.p4c: Slowing the head down ships the fault anyway. Fix it upstream, in the digitising, and it stays fixed for every run.
problems.p5f: Production is too slow to be worth it.
problems.p5c: Stitch count, colour changes and trims are design decisions. A better file runs faster on the same machine.

machineProof.h2: What a first stitch-out actually looks like.
machineProof.sub: Every institute shows you finished work. Here is the part they leave out: the same motif, stitched badly, with the four faults marked and the file change that fixes each one.
machineProof.fileNote: The design as it leaves emCAD: outline, control points and colour blocks. Nothing here has met cloth yet.
machineProof.failedNote: Puckered ground, a thin and gapping fill, the inner line out of register, and a broken thread. Four faults, four different causes.
machineProof.fixNote: Underlay added, density raised, travel order re-cut. Every change is made in the file — not by slowing the machine down.
machineProof.finalNote: The same design, run again. Clean satin, the echo in register, and a piece you would put your name on.
machineProof.foot: These are drawn diagrams of ordinary production faults, not a record of any student's work. Real studio and student photography is being shot.

sts.h2: Watch a file become a stitch.
sts.sub: One motif in three states: the emCAD file, the path the machine follows, and the finished piece. Every course teaches all three, because knowing only one of them is what keeps an operator an operator.
sts.note1: Outline, control points and colour blocks: the design as it leaves the screen.
sts.note2: Travel order, density and where the needle enters. Quality is decided here, not at the machine.
sts.note3: Satin fill, beadwork and finishing, on real fabric.

coursesPage.title: Eleven techniques, taught on the machines that make them.
coursesPage.intro: Three families: machine embroidery, the modern techniques, and the emCAD design software behind both. Start wherever you are — most students arrive having never touched a machine.
facts: Certificate with a verifiable QR code
A free demo class before you commit

pathway.line: The courses connect. Most students start at one machine technique, add emCAD design, and move into production work or a unit of their own.

stages.d: Frames, tension, threading and material — the part that stops your stitches breaking.
Zardosi, 4-beads, sequence, coding or chain and multi. Depth in one before breadth across many.
Make the files the machines run. This is the step that turns an operator into a designer.
Job work, a studio floor, or your own machines and your own clients.

coursesPage.countNote: This catalogue lists {count} courses in three families.

relate.h2: How the three families fit together.
relate.line: They are not three separate schools. A machine technique gives you the hands, the design software gives you control over what the machine is asked to do, and the modern techniques sell alongside both.

points.d: Underlay, density and stitch direction are decided the same way in every machine technique. Learn them once and every other course reads faster.

points.t: The machine techniques are the trade
points.d: Zardosi, beads, sequence, coding, chain and multi are what Surat's units order every day, and each has its own faults to learn.
An operator runs someone's file. A digitiser decides whether the job works before the machine is switched on — and can take digitising work on its own.

points.t: Laser and tufting open other buyers
points.d: Cut-work and tufted pieces sell to boutiques, interior work and gifting, which is a different order book from garment job work.

aboutPage.title: A studio that teaches, and a studio that ships.
aboutPage.intro: Karma is one floor in Mota Varachha doing two things with the same machines: training people who want the skill, and developing embroidery for businesses that need the work done. Neither side is a sideline.
aboutPage.twoSidesSub: This is the part most institutes cannot claim: the trainers are not between jobs, they are between orders.
aboutPage.academyBody: Eleven courses across machine embroidery, the modern techniques and emCAD design. Training happens at the machine from the first session, in Gujarati and Hindi, in morning and evening batches.
aboutPage.labBody: Design development, digitizing and production embroidery for garment businesses. The same machines, the same people, on live commercial work — which is why the teaching stays current.
aboutPage.machinesBody: Every technique taught on this floor, named. Swatches stand in for the studio photographs until the shoot happens — we would rather draw the stitch than borrow someone else’s picture of it.
aboutPage.storyTitle: The story, in the owner’s words
aboutPage.storySub: Three things on this page are the owner’s to say, not ours to write. They are marked, and they stay empty until we have them.
aboutPage.storyBody: The founding story goes here, in the owner’s own words: why Karma started, and what “from design screen to finished stitch” looks like on this floor every day.
aboutPage.karmaBody: What the name and the crown stand for, answered by the person who chose them.
